title: Tuga W8 vs Tuga W10: 8 Inch or 10 Inch Rugged Windows Tablet?
description: Tuga W8 (8 inch, £629) or Tuga W10 (10.1 inch, £649)? £20 apart, so ports, weight and screen decide it. Who needs Ethernet, and who should buy the lighter W8?
summary: £20 apart, both Windows 11 Pro, IP65 and a removable 5000mAh battery: the W8 is 379g lighter with a Full HD 550 nit screen, MIL-STD-810H, and 4G, GPS and NFC built in; the W10 adds a 10.1 inch screen, RJ45 Ethernet and RFID and fingerprint options.
lede: For anyone settled on Windows 11 Pro and choosing between the two Tuga tablets. The short answer: the £20 price gap decides nothing, so buy the Tuga W8 if the tablet is carried and used outdoors, and the Tuga W10 if it plugs into network gear with a cable or needs the bigger screen on a desk or in a vehicle mount.
verdict: Weight and ports decide this one, not price. The Tuga W8 costs £629 and the Tuga W10 £649, a gap of £20 for two tablets that share Windows 11 Pro, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, IP65 sealing, a removable 5000mAh battery and the same tablet accessories. On most of the table the cheaper W8 is ahead: an Intel N150 (up to 3.6GHz) against the W10's Intel N100 (up to 3.4GHz), a 1920 x 1200 screen at 550 nits against 1280 x 800 with no brightness listed, MIL-STD-810H with a 1.22 metre drop rating, a -20°C to 60°C operating range against -10°C to 50°C, Wi-Fi 6 against Wi-Fi 5, and 818g against 1197g. The W10's extra £20 buys a 10.1 inch screen against 8 inch, an RJ45 Ethernet port and a full size HDMI port against the W8's mini HDMI.

Pay the £20, and carry the extra 379g, if the job involves a cable. The W10's 100Mbps RJ45 Ethernet port plugs straight into control panels, switches and plant that have never seen Wi-Fi, and the W8 lists no Ethernet port at all. That is the engineer's and commissioning case, and the larger screen helps there too, with a wiring diagram at 10.1 inches, though at 1280 x 800 it shows things larger rather than in more detail: the W8's smaller screen has more pixels. The W10 also lists a UHF RFID reader and a fingerprint reader as options, and the W8 offers neither.

Do not pay it if the tablet is carried around a site all day, lives in your hands or sits out in the weather: the W8 is the one to buy, and it is the cheaper one too. Both are sealed to IP65, which covers dust and water jets but not immersion. The W8 is tested to MIL-STD-810H with a 1.22 metre drop rating, where the W10 carries its maker's own rating for 1.5 metre drops onto concrete and no MIL-STD rating, and the W8 is rated for colder and hotter conditions, -20°C to 60°C against -10°C to 50°C. It has 4G LTE, GPS and NFC built in, where the W10 lists all three as options. For a tablet that goes up ladders and into plant rooms, that list is a strong reason to choose the W8. Our guide to tablets for field engineers goes through both tablets and how to choose between them.
chooseA: You carry it rather than dock it: the W8 is 379g lighter, at 818g against 1197g.
You work outdoors or in the cold: the W8 lists a 550 nit screen, MIL-STD-810H and a -20°C to 60°C operating range; the W10 lists no brightness or MIL-STD rating and works from -10°C to 50°C.
You need a mobile connection, a position fix and NFC as standard: 4G LTE, GPS and NFC are built into the W8, where the W10 lists all three as options.
You want the sharper screen: 1920 x 1200 on the W8 against 1280 x 800 on the W10.
You photograph every job: the W8's rear camera is listed at 8MP against the W10's 5MP.
chooseB: You plug into panels, switches or plant with a cable: the W10 has an RJ45 Ethernet port and the W8 lists none.
You read wiring diagrams, drawings or spreadsheets on a desk or in a vehicle mount and want them bigger: 10.1 inches against 8, though at 1280 x 800 against the W8's 1920 x 1200.
You sign in with a fingerprint: the W10 lists a fingerprint reader as an option, and the W8 has none.
You tag assets with RFID: the W10 lists an optional UHF RFID reader, and the W8 does not.

faq.q: Is the Tuga W10 worth £20 more than the Tuga W8?
faq.a: Only if the cable or the larger screen matters to you. The W10 costs £649 and the W8 £629, and they share Windows 11 Pro, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, IP65 sealing, a removable 5000mAh battery, USB-C and USB-A. The W10 adds a 10.1 inch screen, RJ45 Ethernet, a full size HDMI port and the options of a UHF RFID reader and a fingerprint reader, and weighs 1197g against 818g. The W8 has the sharper 1920 x 1200 screen at 550 nits, the Intel N150, MIL-STD-810H, the wider operating range and 4G LTE, GPS and NFC as standard. If you do not need the cable or the screen size, buy the Tuga W8. Both include 12 months of warranty, and the paid 3-Year Warranty is £79 on either.

faq.q: Which is tougher, the Tuga W8 or the Tuga W10?
faq.a: On paper, the W8. Both are sealed to IP65, which covers dust and water jets but not immersion, so neither is rated for a dunk in water. The W8 is tested to MIL-STD-810H with a 1.22 metre drop rating and rated to work from -20°C to 60°C. The W10 carries its maker's own rating for 1.5 metre drops onto concrete, with no MIL-STD rating, and works from -10°C to 50°C. The two drop figures come from different tests, so the higher number does not make the W10 the tougher tablet. The W10's case rests on its ports and screen size rather than its ratings. Our MIL-STD-810H guide explains what the rating does and does not tell you, and the IP rating guide covers what IP65 means in practice.

faq.q: Does the Tuga W10 have 4G and GPS like the W8?
faq.a: As options, not as standard. The W8 has 4G LTE, GPS and NFC built in, alongside dual-band Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2. The W10's listed connectivity is dual-band Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.2 and 100Mbps Ethernet, with 4G LTE, GPS and NFC listed as options without prices, so the standard W10 is a Wi-Fi and cable tablet; ask us before you order if you need any of them. The same goes for the W10's optional fingerprint reader, which the W8 does not offer. If the tablet needs its own mobile connection in the van and a position fix without a phone hotspot, the W8 has both built in. Both tablets fit the Vehicle Mounting Dock (£109) and the 12V DC Car Charger (£26) on the accessories page.

faq.q: Can I get the Tuga W8 or W10 with a barcode scanner?
faq.a: Yes, both. The Tuga W8 with 2D Scanner is £699, £70 more than the standard W8, and reads QR codes, Data Matrix and PDF417. The Tuga W10 with 2D Scanner is £729, £80 more than the standard W10, and its Newland scan engine reads 1D barcodes plus QR, PDF417, Aztec and MaxiCode. The scanner versions are £30 apart. Each is sold from the same product page as its base model, the W8 page or the W10 page. The W10 also lists a UHF RFID reader as an option, which the W8 does not, so if you tag pallets or tools with RFID rather than barcodes, the W10 is the one to ask about. For a handful of scans a day, a scanning app using the camera may be enough, and you should check that the app runs on the device before relying on it; our guide to built-in barcode scanners explains 1D, 2D and RFID and when the extra cost pays off.
